properties.title: A Physiology-Informed Digital Twin Framework for Simulating Liver Health Progression

membership.reason: HEPATWIN is a physiology-informed mechanistic liver digital twin simulating multi-year biomarker trajectories under patient-specific diet and activity inputs.
membership.counting_boundary: Verified L1 longitudinal organ digital twin (WT_ORGAN, BP_FORECAST); lifestyle conditioning implemented but not evaluated under controlled action variation.

properties.backbone: Systems-level mechanistic hepatic physiology simulator with stage-transition-driven calibration (NAFLD/fibrosis/cirrhosis)

properties.flow: Diet, physical activity, demographics, baseline biomarkers -> HEPATWIN mechanistic liver modules -> multi-year ALT/ALP/albumin/bilirubin trajectories -> NASH detection

properties.purpose: Longitudinal simulation of liver function, early-stage NAFLD/NASH progression, and biomarker estimation.

assertions.rationale: Persistent physiological hepatic state (glycogen, lipids, bilirubin, etc.) evolving over configurable multi-year days.
Patient-specific dietary intake and physical activity lifestyle inputs.

Hybrid physiology-informed mechanistic hepatic modules combined with a data-driven statistical regression mapping (fitted on the Cirrhosis Patient Survival dataset plus healthy reference ranges) that computes a stage-transition progress factor p = f_prog(D_pre, D_post) applied as a baseline-referenced drift correction B^(t+1) = B_tilde^(t+1) + (p - 1)B^(t).
Simulates biomarker evolution under varying patient-specific dietary and activity conditions.
Mechanistic systems-level liver physiology (metabolism, VLDL export, urea, bile, bilirubin conjugation).

Evaluated longitudinal follow-up biomarker prediction on NIDDK NAFLD patients: Table III (2 visits, single 48-week follow-up step, n=199) reports R^2 from 0.13 (AST) to 0.60 (Direct Bilirubin) and MAE 0.07-21.01; Tables IV-VI extend to 3-5 visits (~5 years), where AST R^2 degrades to -0.15.
Early-stage liver disease monitoring and NASH detection.
Multi-year longitudinal biomarker trajectory accuracy against NIDDK NAFLD follow-up visits.
Downstream NASH detection using HEPATWIN-simulated biomarkers vs ground-truth lab models.

evidence_fragments.content:
Abstract— We present a physiology-informed digital twin
of the human liver designed for longitudinal simulation
of liver function and early-stage disease progression.
The model, referred to asHEPATWIN, integrates key hep-
atic processes, including carbohydrate, lipid, and protein
metabolism, bilirubin conjugation, bile production, and
detoxification, within a unified systems-level framework
to generate clinically observable biomarker trajectories.
Unlike purely data-driven approaches,HEPATWINincorpo-
rates mechanistic representations of liver physiology and
patient-specific inputs such as diet, activity, and base-
line biomarkers to simulate disease evolution over time.
To ensure consistency with clinical progression patterns,
we introduce a stage-transition-driven calibration mecha-
nism that aligns simulated outputs with population-level
biomarker distributions across disease stages, including
NAFLD, fibrosis, and cirrhosis. Validation using the NIDDK
NAFLD dataset demonstrates thatHEPATWINproduces lon-
gitudinal biomarker estimates within clinically acceptable
ranges and can forecast trajectories over multi-year hori-
zons. Furthermore, simulated biomarkers retain sufficient
clinical signal to support downstream NASH detection with
competitive performance relative to models using ground-
truth laboratory data. These results highlight the potential
of physiology-informed digital twins for personalized, non-
invasive diagnosis and prediction of organ health in general
and liver health monitoring in particular.

locator.section_or_table: Section IV: Methodology Overview—HEPATWIN Design and Validation

evidence_fragments.content:
HEPATWINis a physiology-driven liver digital twin de-
signed to simulate key liver functions using patient-specific
information, such as dietary intake, demographic and physical
profile, activity level, and baseline liver biomarker values. The
model captures core hepatic processes—such as metabolism,
protein synthesis, bilirubin conjugation, bile production, and
detoxification, while incorporating contextual interactions with
other organs, including the gallbladder, pancreas, skeletal
muscle, and adipose tissue. Based on the input information,
HEPATWINperforms the core functions and generates updated
liver biomarker values (ALT, ALP, albumin, and bilirubin) that
reflect the evolving physiological state of the liver over time.
Each simulation instance represents longitudinal changes
in liver health over a configurable number of days, where
the duration can be dynamically defined based on the speci-
fied dietary and lifestyle conditions. The resulting simulated
biomarkers are subsequently used for further analysis, includ-
ing disease stage assessment such as NASH detection. By
combining physiology-based simulation with patient context,
HEPATWINenables personalized modeling of liver disease
progression and supports early, non-invasive monitoring in
precision medicine settings.

locator.section_or_table: Section V-E: Biomarker Trajectory Estimation (stage-transition statistical regression calibration)

evidence_fragments.content:

mechanistic biomarker estimates based on simulated hepatic
function, population-level disease stage transition patterns are
incorporated through a stage-transition–driven calibration step.
To construct stage-consistent biomarker reference distribu-
tions, we utilize the Cirrhosis Patient Survival dataset, which
provides cirrhosis stage–specific biomarker values (Stages 1–
3) [30]. Healthy reference ranges are integrated with this
dataset, sample sizes are balanced, and a statistical regression
mapping is developed to estimate biomarker distributions for
intermediate disease stages, including NAFLD and Fibrosis.
Fig. 7 illustrates the safe ranges for each biomarker (bilirubin,
ALT, ALP, albumin), the observed distributions for healthy and
cirrhosis stages, and the estimated distributions for intermedi-
ate stages [4]. Once the physiology simulation is completed,
the pre-physiology disease stateD pre and post-physiology
disease stateD post are used to compute a progress factor
p=f prog(D pre, Dpost)using the stage-specific biomarker
mapping derived from the dataset. This progress factor repre-
sents the direction and magnitude of disease progression or
recovery over the simulated interval.
The final biomarker estimate is obtained by applying a
baseline-referenced drift correction to the mechanistic output:
B(t+1) = ˜B(t+1) + (p−1)B (t)
Here ˜B(t+1) is the mechanistic estimate generated by
the physiology module in Algorithm 1,B t is the baseline
biomarker value provided as input toHEPATWIN, andpis
the stage-transition–driven progress factor. WhenD pre=Dpost,
p= 1, and the final estimated value equals the mechanistic
output. When disease severity increases,p >1, producing
an upward drift relative to baseline; conversely, when disease
severity improves,p <1, resulting in a downward adjustment.

locator.section_or_table: Section VI-C & VII: NASH detection & hybrid physiology + data-driven calibration

evidence_fragments.content:
In the second experiment, we assess whether the estimated
biomarker trajectories generated byHEPATWINretain suffi-
cient clinical signal for NASH detection. First, we establish
a baseline by using ground truth biomarker values from the
NIDDK dataset to detect NASH status. Using time-series
ground truth biomarker values, the detection model achieves
a performance of Accuracy: 0.76, Precision: 0.78, Recall:
0.71, F1-score: 0.75. These results are consistent with existing
statistical approaches on the same dataset, where models
trained using biopsy-day biomarker values achieve approxi-
mately 75% accuracy [32].
Next, we replace ground truth biomarker trajectories with
HEPATWIN-estimated biomarker trajectories and repeat the
NASH detection task. Using the estimated time-series data,
the detection accuracy is 65%. Most existing models trained
on the same dataset estimate NASH status using biomarker
measurements collected at or near the biopsy visit, where the
pathological state of the liver is already reflected in the labora-
tory values. In contrast,HEPATWINachieves this65% NASH
detection accuracyusingbaseline lifestyle and demographic
information to generate longitudinal biomarker trajectories
that extend up tofive years into the future. Achieving 65%
detection accuracy under this long-horizon prediction setting
indicates that the physiology-driven digital twin preserves clin-
ically meaningful disease signals over extended time intervals,
demonstrating the practical value ofHEPATWINfor early
risk assessment and long-term liver health monitoring. These
findings suggest that even approximate biomarker trajectories
derived fromHEPATWINpreserve sufficient disease-related
signal to support downstream NASH classification.

capability_assessments.rationale: Downgraded honestly from L2 to L1: HEPATWIN implements hybrid mechanistic + data-driven stage-transition-calibrated dynamics and evaluates longitudinal biomarker forecasting over 2-5 visits (48-week intervals up to ~5 years) on 825 NIDDK NAFLD patients (L1). Although patient-specific dietary intake and physical activity are explicit simulator inputs (dynamics.action_conditioned at implementation), validation uses only passive observed baseline covariates without controlled lifestyle perturbation, ablation, or alternative-intervention comparison; thus L2 is not demonstrated (matching legacy column Z = L1 Temporal prediction).

readiness_assessments.legacy_highest_label: R2 Retrospective NIDDK NAFLD cohort validation

limitations: Single cohort (NIDDK NAFLD, n=825 with >=2 visits) retrospective validation; no prospective clinical deployment.

Dietary intake and physical activity are modeled as baseline simulator inputs, but no controlled lifestyle intervention, counterfactual comparison, or input ablation is evaluated; demonstrated capability is L1 (not L2).
Transaminase R^2 degrades at extended horizons (AST R^2 = -0.15 at 5 visits); no persistence or simple baseline comparison is reported for biomarker forecasting.
notes: All 15 physical PDF pages extracted/read; page 4 visually inspected via rendered PNG.

legacy_cells.B: A Physiology-Informed Digital Twin Framework for Simulating Liver Health Progression
legacy_cells.C: Sumaiya Afroz Mila, and Sandip Ray, Senior Member, IEEE
legacy_cells.O: Nonalcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD), nonalcoholic steatohepatitis (NASH), and fibrosis
legacy_cells.S: Can screening-day patient, lifestyle, and biomarker inputs yield multi-visit forecasts of liver biomarkers and support downstream NASH detection?
legacy_cells.T: NIDDK NAFLD Adult dataset participants; 825 retained with at least two visits from an initial 1,410
legacy_cells.AI: Structured tabular demographics (age, gender, height, weight); lifestyle/diet (activity level and hours, sitting hours, daily calories, protein, carbohydrate, and fat intake); screening-visit liver biomarkers (total/direct bilirubin, albumin, AST, ALT, ALP)
legacy_cells.AZ: Explicit process variables include glycogen storage, liver/adipose fat, hepatocyte capacity, damage, inflammation, cholestasis, and bile/bilirubin pools
legacy_cells.BD: Daily calories; carbohydrate, protein, and fat intake; activity level and activity/sitting hours; demographic/profile and baseline biomarkers are also model inputs
legacy_cells.BL: Longitudinal simulation over configurable days; clinical follow-up visits at weeks 48, 96, 144, and 192
legacy_cells.BN: Physiology-encoded nutrient allocation and storage; glycogen-capacity constraints; bilirubin conjugation efficiency bounded to 0.05–0.90; stage-specific biomarker trend calibration
legacy_cells.BS: Longitudinal estimates of ALT, AST, ALP, albumin, total bilirubin, and direct bilirubin
legacy_cells.BT: Biomarker outputs; a separate downstream ML inference pipeline classifies NASH from estimated biomarker trajectories
legacy_cells.CD: Up to five follow-up visits (approximately five years)
legacy_cells.DN: NIDDK NAFLD Adult dataset; Cirrhosis Patient Survival dataset
legacy_cells.DQ: 1,410 initial dataset participants; 825 retained participants with at least two visits
legacy_cells.DY: Multi-step forecasting was evaluated over 2–5 follow-up visits. At five follow-up visits (n=772), reported MAE: AST 17.38, ALT 22.24, ALP 19.79, albumin 0.29, total bilirubin 0.28, direct bilirubin 0.08 (table does not state units).
legacy_cells.EC: Downstream NASH classification: 76% accuracy (precision 0.78, recall 0.71, F1 0.75) using ground-truth time-series biomarkers; 65% accuracy using HEPATWIN-estimated time-series biomarkers.
legacy_cells.EI: Same downstream NASH classifier: accuracy 0.76 with ground-truth time-series biomarkers versus 0.65 with HEPATWIN-estimated trajectories; authors also cite approximately 75% for prior biopsy-day biomarker models.
legacy_cells.EL: AST/ALT errors varied more at extended horizons; authors attribute this partly to inflammation-driven nonlinear fluctuations not fully captured and note AST also comes from cardiac and skeletal muscle.
legacy_cells.FL: Patient-specific demographic, lifestyle/diet, and screening biomarker inputs feed physiology-based liver modules and explicit evolving process variables; stage-transition calibration adjusts estimated biomarker trajectories; a separate ML pipeline evaluates NASH detection. No action planner is evaluated.
legacy_cells.FM: Introduces HEPATWIN, a physiology-informed liver digital twin with integrated hepatic process modules, stage-transition-based biomarker calibration, longitudinal validation, and downstream NASH detection using generated biomarkers.
legacy_cells.FN: NIDDK validation reports longitudinal biomarker forecasts up to approximately five years; at five follow-up visits, total bilirubin MAE was 0.28 and direct bilirubin MAE 0.08. NASH detection accuracy was 0.65 with simulated trajectories versus 0.76 with ground-truth time-series biomarkers.
legacy_cells.FO: Authors report greater AST/ALT variability at extended horizons, likely from inflammation-driven nonlinear fluctuations not fully captured; AST is not liver-specific and muscle/cardiac sources add variability.
legacy_cells.FP: Future work: add inter-organ interactions and adaptive feedback mechanisms to improve physiological realism and personalized lifestyle guidance.
legacy_cells.FQ: Authors identify limited physiology-informed digital twins for stage-specific biomarker estimation under data scarcity, and prior work lacking integrated liver functions and longitudinal transitions across disease stages.
legacy_cells.FR: The results support retrospective multi-visit biomarker forecasting and a downstream NASH classification experiment, not prospective benefit, external generalization, or identified individual causal effects of changed lifestyle actions. Lifestyle inputs are modeled, but alternative action sequences are not compared as causal counterfactuals and no planning/control results are shown.
legacy_cells.FS: Reviewer mapping: M3 Belief-state service; M4 Action service; M5 Dynamics adapter; M6 Rollout service; M7 Outcome & causal layer
legacy_cells.FT: Reviewer lesson: Expose future-state forecasts through a time-aware dynamics interface and validate error versus horizon; treatment actions need separate evidence before intervention simulation.
legacy_cells.FX: Full 15-page extracted text read, including title/abstract and Introduction (pp. 1–2), Related Work (pp. 2–3), physiology background (pp. 3–4), design/methods and algorithms (pp. 4–11), Tables I–VI and dataset/validation results (pp. 11–14), Conclusion and data availability (p. 14); references and author bios also read (pp. 14–15). No separate limitations section; limitations are reported in the results discussion. | Codex audit: title/byline, abstract/conclusion, targeted methods/results and cross-check of prior quotations against extracted full text. This is a targeted audit, not an independent re-extraction of every negative/unreported field.
legacy_cells.FZ: Prefilled A:I were left untouched except C: the PDF byline directly specifies the author names/order and was used verbatim. HEPATWIN explicitly conditions on patient lifestyle inputs, but results do not compare alternative intervention sequences; demonstrated capability is therefore L1, with L2 recorded only as the authors' claim. No causal identification of lifestyle effects or planning is demonstrated. Table extraction has flattened/wrapped columns; values recorded from clearly legible Table VI MAE rows and explicit text. Evidence QA: 25/64 populated fields had a <=25-word quotation matching extracted PDF text (39.1%). Confidence is conservative; review this row where exact quote checks were incomplete. Codex audit: 59 prior populated fields have a located source quotation; 6 have quotations not located by normalized text matching. Unlocated quotations are review flags, not proof that the value is false. Companion evidence audit lists affected columns. Reviewer FS/FT/FU mappings are synthesis. Prior unsupported/missing fields remain Not reported; no clinical benefit inferred from offline simulation.
